definition: Didactic means intended to instruct, with a lecturing or moralizing tone.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word didactic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know didactic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The gardening column turned didactic this spring, capping each entry with a numbered lesson on discipline.
Informative is milder than didactic — an informative piece hands you facts and lets you be; nothing is pressed.
Sermonizing goes further than didactic: didactic work at least means to teach, while sermonizing has given up teaching for pure moral scolding.

Moralizing work pushes judgments of right and wrong at its audience — every scene closes on a verdict about how to live. Didactic is wider: a didactic book is built to instruct, and the lesson it presses may be moral, practical, or technical. All moralizing is pushy teaching; not all didactic teaching moralizes.

Lecturing is instruction delivered at you whether or not you asked — the word catches a speaker's manner in the moment. Didactic describes design rather than delivery: a work is didactic because it was built to improve its audience, even when its tone stays gentle from page to page.

Didactic means built to instruct, and it usually carries a whiff of heavy-handedness: the lesson is pressed on you.
It is narrower than pedagogical, which describes teaching methods neutrally, and stronger than informative — didactic work wants you improved, not merely informed.

Didactic judges tone where pedagogical describes craft: a pedagogical choice concerns how teaching works, while calling a work didactic says it pushes its lesson at you — praise in a textbook, a complaint in a film review.

The old signs along the canyon trail gave distances and warnings and nothing else.
After the redesign, hikers noticed the difference at the first switchback: each new sign poses a question, answers it, and assigns a small task -- count the rings, find the flood line.
The ranger who wrote them is unapologetic about the purpose.
The trail, she says, is a classroom now; a sign that does not teach something has failed.
A columnist grumbled that the canyon had turned didactic, every bend pressing its lesson, and hikers could no longer simply look.
Attendance at the junior ranger program, the park notes, has doubled since the signs went up.
